title: THEY BELIEVED IN JESUS… SO WHY DID THE CHURCH STILL QUESTION WHETHER THEY BELONGED?
paragraphs: THEY BELIEVED IN JESUS… SO WHY DID THE CHURCH STILL QUESTION WHETHER THEY BELONGED?
The explosive controversy in Acts 15 that nearly divided the early Church—and the breathtaking truth about grace, salvation, and the religious burdens Jesus never asked you to carry.
Imagine giving your life to Jesus Christ.

You have repented of your sins. You believe He died for you. You believe God raised Him from the dead. Your old life is beginning to change. For the first time, you understand what it means to be forgiven.
And then someone walks into your church and tells you something devastating.
“Your faith in Jesus is not enough.”
Not because you refuse to repent.
Not because you reject God's Word.
Not because you are deliberately living in rebellion.
But because you have not undergone a religious ritual that someone insists is necessary before God can truly accept you.
Suddenly, the joy of salvation becomes a question.
Am I really saved?
Have I done enough?
What if Jesus has forgiven me, but God is still waiting for something else?
Now imagine that this is not a modern church argument.
It is happening in the first century, while apostles who personally knew Jesus are still alive.
And the question is so serious that church leaders must gather in Jerusalem to confront it.
Because beneath the controversy over circumcision and the Law of Moses lies a question that reaches into every generation of Christianity.
Is Jesus Christ sufficient to save a sinner, or must something be added to His finished work?
This is the controversy recorded in Acts 15:1–29.

And if you have ever felt that you must earn God's acceptance, prove your worthiness, or become religious enough before you can truly belong to Him, what happened in Jerusalem may change how you understand the Gospel forever.
Because the early Church was about to discover something that many Christians still struggle to believe.
The grace that saves you is not a reward for becoming worthy. It is God's mercy toward people who could never make themselves worthy.
But to understand why this controversy became so explosive, we must first understand something many modern readers overlook.
The people arguing about the Law of Moses were not simply arguing about ancient religious customs.
They were arguing about identity.
Covenant.
Holiness.
Belonging.
And what it meant for Israel's promised Messiah to become the Savior of the nations.
For centuries, the Jewish people had lived under the covenant God established with Israel through Moses.
The Law shaped their worship, their community, their festivals, their food practices, and their understanding of covenant faithfulness.
Circumcision, however, reached even further back than Moses.
In Genesis 17, God commanded Abraham and his male descendants to receive circumcision as the sign of His covenant.
It was not an insignificant custom.
It was deeply connected to Israel's history and identity as God's covenant people.
So when Gentiles—people from the nations outside Israel—began believing in Jesus without first becoming Jewish proselytes, a profound question emerged.
If these Gentiles worshiped Israel's God and followed Israel's Messiah, did they also have to adopt Israel's covenant markers?
Did they have to be circumcised?
Did they have to keep the Mosaic Law?
And if they refused, could they really be considered saved?
Some believers answered yes.
Acts 15:1 records their teaching:
“Except ye be circumcised after the manner of Moses, ye cannot be saved.” (KJV)
Read those final words again.
“Ye cannot be saved.”
That was the heart of the controversy.
It was not merely a discussion about whether certain Jewish customs were valuable.
It was a claim that Gentile believers could not receive salvation without circumcision according to the Mosaic custom.
And that claim struck directly at the Gospel Paul and Barnabas had been proclaiming.
Because Gentiles were already coming to faith in Jesus.
God was already transforming their lives.
The Holy Spirit was already at work among them.
Yet now some were insisting that something else had to happen before their salvation could be recognized.
Can you imagine the confusion?
A Gentile believer who had once worshiped idols now worshiped the living God.
A man who had never known the Scriptures of Israel now loved the Messiah promised within them.
A woman who had lived without the hope of Christ now rejoiced in His resurrection.
And suddenly they were hearing that faith in Jesus was not sufficient.
That they needed another qualification.
Another requirement.
Another condition.
The question was no longer theoretical.
It concerned real people whose confidence in the Gospel was being shaken.
And perhaps that is why this ancient controversy still feels painfully familiar.
Because religious pressure has a way of changing its clothing without changing its voice.
Today, someone may not tell you that you must be circumcised to be saved.

But you may hear that you cannot truly belong to Christ unless you follow a particular denomination's traditions, observe certain customs, or meet standards that Scripture never establishes as conditions of salvation.
You may begin to measure God's acceptance by how perfectly you perform.
You may confuse spiritual maturity with earning justification.
You may even begin treating obedience as the price of God's love rather than the fruit of His grace.
And before long, your relationship with Jesus becomes an exhausting attempt to prove that you deserve what He came to give.
But Acts 15 forces us to confront the issue.
When human requirements are made conditions of salvation, the sufficiency of Christ is placed in question.
Paul and Barnabas understood what was at stake.
Acts 15:2 says there was “no small dissension and disputation” between them and those promoting this teaching.
In other words, this was not a quiet disagreement.
It was a serious confrontation.
The church in Antioch therefore appointed Paul, Barnabas, and others to travel to Jerusalem to discuss the matter with the apostles and elders.
Picture that journey.
These missionaries had witnessed Gentiles turning from idols to the living God.
They had seen the power of the Gospel crossing ethnic, cultural, and religious boundaries.
And now they were traveling toward the very city where Jesus had been crucified and raised from the dead, carrying a question that would shape the Church's understanding of Gentile inclusion.
When they arrived, they reported what God had done among the Gentiles.
But the controversy did not disappear.
Acts 15:5 records that some believers from the party of the Pharisees stood up and declared that Gentile converts needed to be circumcised and commanded to keep the Law of Moses.
Notice something important.
Luke identifies these people as believers.
This was a dispute arising within the Christian community.
And that matters.
Because sincere religious conviction does not automatically guarantee correct biblical understanding.
A person may genuinely believe that they are defending holiness while mistakenly placing a burden on others that the Gospel does not require.
That does not mean holiness is unimportant.
It means we must never confuse the foundation of salvation with the obedience that flows from salvation.
Then Peter stood up.
And what he said went straight to the heart of the matter.
He reminded the assembly that God had already chosen to bring the Gospel to the Gentiles through his ministry.
This pointed back to the events recorded in Acts 10, when Peter entered the household of Cornelius, a Gentile centurion.
Cornelius was not presented as someone who had first become Jewish through circumcision.
Yet as Peter proclaimed Jesus Christ, the Holy Spirit fell upon those who heard the message.
God Himself had demonstrated that Gentiles could receive the Spirit through faith in Christ.
Peter had witnessed it.
And now he was asking the Jerusalem assembly to recognize what God had already made clear.
Acts 15:8–9 says:
“And God, which knoweth the hearts, bare them witness, giving them the Holy Ghost, even as he did unto us; And put no difference between us and them, purifying their hearts by faith.” (KJV)
“Purifying their hearts by faith.”
In the Greek text, the phrase is:
τῇ πίστει καθαρίσας τὰς καρδίας αὐτῶν
Tē pistei katharisas tas kardias autōn.
Meaning, in context:
“Having cleansed their hearts by faith.”
The Greek verb καθαρίσας (katharisas) comes from katharizō, meaning to cleanse or purify.
Peter's point was extraordinary.
God had already cleansed the hearts of Gentile believers through faith.
He had not waited for them to adopt circumcision as a prerequisite for receiving the Holy Spirit.
He had not treated their ethnicity as a barrier to His saving grace.
The God who knows the human heart had accepted them.
And if God had already received them through Christ, on what basis could the Church demand an additional condition for salvation?
Then Peter asked a question that should make every religious leader examine the burdens they place upon people.
Acts 15:10:
“Now therefore why tempt ye God, to put a yoke upon the neck of the disciples, which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear?” (KJV)
A yoke.
Imagine a heavy wooden beam placed across the shoulders of an animal to carry or pull a burden.
That is the picture Peter used.
He was not calling God's Law evil.
Scripture elsewhere describes the Law as holy, righteous, and good (Romans 7:12).
The problem was not that God had given Israel His Law.
The problem was demanding the Mosaic covenant's requirements as a condition for Gentiles to be saved.
Israel's history had already demonstrated humanity's inability to establish righteousness before God through flawless law-keeping.
And now some wanted to place that burden upon Gentile disciples.
Peter challenged them.
Why impose upon these believers a requirement that cannot accomplish what only God's grace can accomplish?
Then came the declaration that stands at the center of the entire passage.
Acts 15:11:
“But we believe that through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ we shall be saved, even as they.” (KJV)
Do not miss the beauty of Peter's wording.
He did not simply say that Gentiles could be saved like Jews.
He said that Jewish believers would be saved through the grace of Jesus Christ, just as Gentile believers would.
The ground was level at the cross.
The religiously educated Jew needed grace.
The Gentile who had once worshiped idols needed grace.
The apostle needed grace.
The former Pharisee needed grace.
The person raised hearing the Scriptures needed grace.
And the person hearing about Jesus for the first time needed that same grace.
No ethnicity could purchase salvation.
No ancestry could secure justification.
No religious achievement could replace the saving work of Christ.
There was one Savior for both Jew and Gentile.
The Greek text of Acts 15:11 reads:
ἀλλὰ διὰ τῆς χάριτος τοῦ κυρίου Ἰησοῦ πιστεύομεν σωθῆναι καθ᾽ ὃν τρόπον κἀκεῖνοι.
Alla dia tēs charitos tou kyriou Iēsou pisteuomen sōthēnai kath’ hon tropon kakeinoi.
The essential meaning is:
“But we believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they are.”
The word χάριτος (charitos) is the genitive form of charis, commonly translated “grace.”
In this passage, grace is not a vague feeling of divine kindness.
It is God's saving favor through the Lord Jesus Christ.
And the verb σωθῆναι (sōthēnai) means “to be saved.”
Peter's argument was not that obedience no longer mattered.
It was that salvation comes through the grace of Christ, not through requiring Gentiles to enter the Mosaic covenant.
That distinction is essential.
Because the Gospel does not teach that Jesus saves us so we can celebrate sin.
It teaches that Jesus saves sinners who cannot rescue themselves, forgives them, and calls them into a transformed life.
Grace is not permission to remain enslaved to sin.
Grace is the mercy of God that brings us into a new relationship with Him and teaches us to live differently.
Titus 2:11–12 explains that God's grace brings salvation and trains believers to reject ungodliness.
Ephesians 2:8–10 teaches that salvation is by grace through faith, not the result of works, and that believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Do you see the order?
We are not saved because our good works make us worthy.
We are saved by grace, and that grace produces a life increasingly shaped by obedience.
Good works are the fruit of salvation, not the price of admission into God's family.
This is where the message becomes deeply personal.
Because some of us have spent years living as though Jesus is continually waiting for us to earn what He already purchased through His death and resurrection.
We confess our sins, but secretly wonder whether God has grown tired of forgiving us.
We pray, but feel ashamed because yesterday we failed again.
We read Scripture, but instead of seeing the beauty of Christ, we see only how far we still have to grow.
We compare ourselves with believers who seem more disciplined, more knowledgeable, more spiritually mature.
And somewhere in that comparison, we begin to believe that God's mercy must be reserved for people who perform better than we do.
But hear this carefully.
If you belong to Jesus Christ, your hope does not rest in the perfection of your spiritual performance.
It rests in the perfection of your Savior.
That does not make repentance unnecessary.
It makes genuine repentance possible without pretending that you can save yourself.
You can confess your sin honestly because Christ is sufficient.
You can turn away from what is destroying you because God's grace is powerful.
You can pursue holiness without imagining that your obedience is somehow completing an unfinished cross.
Jesus did not die to make salvation partially available, leaving the rest for you to earn.
He died and rose again as the sufficient Savior of His people.
And when you fall, the answer is not to abandon repentance or excuse your sin.
The answer is to return to Him in faith.
The One who calls you to holiness is also the One who provides mercy for repentant sinners.
After Peter spoke, the assembly listened as Paul and Barnabas described the signs and wonders God had performed among the Gentiles.
Then James addressed the gathering.
His contribution was crucial because he showed that Gentile inclusion was not a contradiction of God's revealed purposes.
It was consistent with the prophetic Scriptures.
James referred to the prophets, particularly the restoration language found in Amos 9:11–12.
Acts 15:16–17 includes these words:

“After this I will return, and will build again the tabernacle of David, which is fallen down... That the residue of men might seek after the Lord, and all the Gentiles, upon whom my name is called...” (KJV)
The wording James used reflects the Greek scriptural tradition associated with Amos, while the Hebrew Masoretic wording of Amos 9:12 differs in significant details.
That textual distinction deserves honesty.
The Hebrew passage speaks of the restored Davidic kingdom possessing the remnant of Edom and the nations called by God's name.
The Greek form emphasizes the remaining people and the Gentiles seeking the Lord.
These textual traditions are not identical in wording, and scholars discuss their relationship.
But James's central argument in Acts is unmistakable.
God's promises concerning the restoration of David's fallen house were consistent with the inclusion of Gentiles among His people.
Jesus, the promised Son of David, had come.
And the nations were being brought to the Lord through Him.
What looked to some like a threat to Israel's identity was actually part of God's long-declared redemptive purpose.
The Messiah was not abandoning God's promises.
He was fulfilling them.
And that is one of the most beautiful realities of the Gospel.
God's plan of redemption was always greater than one nation.
When God called Abraham, He promised that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him (Genesis 12:3).
The prophets anticipated the nations coming to know the Lord.
And in Jesus Christ, the promised blessing reaches people from every tribe, language, people, and nation.
The Gentiles were not an unexpected interruption in God's plan.
Their inclusion testified to the greatness of His mercy.
Then James offered his judgment.
Acts 15:19:
“Wherefore my sentence is, that we trouble not them, which from among the Gentiles are turned to God.” (KJV)
“That we trouble not them.”
What a remarkable statement.
James was not proposing that Gentile Christians should be left without moral guidance.
He was saying they should not be burdened with the requirement of becoming circumcised and keeping the Mosaic Law as a condition of belonging to Christ.
But the story does not end there.
And this is where a careless reading of Acts 15 can lead to another serious misunderstanding.
Because James also recommended that Gentile believers abstain from certain practices.
Acts 15:20 identifies four areas: things polluted by idols, sexual immorality, things strangled, and blood.
The final letter repeats these instructions in Acts 15:29.
Why?
If salvation is by grace, why give any commands at all?
Because grace does not eliminate the need for faithful Christian living.
And because the early Church was learning how Jewish and Gentile believers could live together as one community under Jesus Christ.
The command to abstain from sexual immorality reflected the continuing importance of sexual holiness.
The Greek term πορνεία (porneia) refers broadly to sexual immorality, with its precise scope understood within the biblical moral context.

The instructions concerning idol-associated food, blood, and strangled animals addressed practices especially sensitive in communities where Jewish and Gentile believers were learning to share fellowship.
Scholars debate whether the four prohibitions primarily reflect Leviticus 17–18, concerns about table fellowship, separation from pagan worship, or a combination of these factors.
The text does not settle every historical question.
But it clearly distinguishes the issue of salvation from the practical responsibilities of believers living together.
The apostles were not saying:
“You are saved by grace, but these four practices will purchase your salvation.”
They were instructing Gentile Christians how to live faithfully and avoid conduct that would compromise holiness or fracture fellowship.
And the letter itself describes these requirements as necessary, not as a new system for earning righteousness.
This matters today.
Because there are two opposite errors that can distort the Gospel.
One says, “Jesus is not enough. You must earn salvation through religious performance.”
The other says, “Because Jesus saves by grace, obedience no longer matters.”
Neither reflects the full teaching of Scripture.
Jesus Christ saves by grace through faith.
And those who belong to Him are called to repent, love God, love their neighbors, flee sexual immorality, reject idolatry, and walk in the Spirit.
Not to purchase salvation.
But because the Savior who forgives also transforms.
Grace does not compete with holiness. Grace leads us into holiness.
The Jerusalem council's decision was then communicated through a letter carried by trusted representatives, including Judas called Barsabbas and Silas, alongside Paul and Barnabas.
And there is a sentence in that letter that deserves our attention.
Acts 15:28:
“For it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us, to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things.” (KJV)
Notice the humility and seriousness.
The leaders did not treat the question as a popularity contest.
They sought to recognize what God had already done among the Gentiles, interpret it in light of Scripture, and give a judgment that protected the Gospel and the fellowship of the Church.
They did not erase the distinction between Jewish and Gentile backgrounds.
They did not declare Israel's Scriptures irrelevant.
They did not teach that Christians could live however they pleased.
They refused to impose circumcision and the Mosaic Law as prerequisites for Gentile salvation.
And when the letter reached Antioch, Acts 15:31 tells us the believers rejoiced because of its encouragement.
Imagine that moment.
The letter is opened.
The congregation listens.
And the Gentile believers who had been troubled by claims that their faith was insufficient hear the decision.
They are not required to become Jewish proselytes in order to be saved through Jesus Christ.
The grace of the Lord Jesus is sufficient.
The Spirit's work among them is recognized.
They are called to live faithfully as members of the community of believers.
And the burden that had threatened their assurance is lifted.
No wonder they rejoiced.
Yet there is another truth here that should make us examine ourselves.
Sometimes the greatest danger to a struggling believer is not an obvious denial of Jesus.
Sometimes it is a message that speaks highly of Jesus while quietly adding human requirements to His saving work.
“Jesus saves, but only if you belong to our particular tradition.”
“Jesus forgives, but you must prove yourself worthy before you can approach Him.”
“Jesus accepts repentant sinners, but your past makes you permanently disqualified.”
Those claims may sound religious.
They may even sound serious about holiness.
But if they make something other than Christ's saving work a necessary ground of justification before God, they distort the Gospel.
The New Testament does call believers to examine their faith, persevere, and demonstrate repentance through transformed lives.
It also warns against empty professions of faith that produce no obedience.
But these truths must never be twisted into the claim that our works are the meritorious foundation of salvation.
Only Jesus can bear that weight.
And perhaps someone reading this has been carrying a weight that was never meant to be the foundation of their hope.
You love God.
You want to obey Him.
But you have become so consumed with your failures that you no longer know how to rest in His mercy.
You have mistaken conviction for condemnation.
You have confused the Holy Spirit's call to repentance with the accusation that Christ could never receive someone like you.
You remember the things you did before you came to faith.
The relationships you damaged.
The lies you told.
The compromises you made.
The moments you knew what was right and chose what was wrong.
And you wonder whether the Gospel could really be good news for someone with your history.
But consider the people Jesus called.
Peter denied Him.
Paul persecuted His followers.
The Corinthian church included people who had come out of deeply sinful ways of life.
Yet Paul wrote to those believers:
“And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God.” (1 Corinthians 6:11, KJV)
“And such were some of you.”
Not because their sins were harmless.
Not because repentance was optional.
But because Jesus Christ truly saves and transforms sinners.
Your past may explain some of your scars.
It does not have the authority to overrule the Gospel.
Your failures may call you to confession, repentance, reconciliation, and renewed obedience.
They do not make Jesus powerless to forgive.
And the scandal of your former life does not have to become the final sentence of your story.
That is why we keep returning to this truth:
Not because He pretends sin never happened.
Not because consequences always disappear.
Not because repentance is unnecessary.
But because through His death and resurrection, Jesus offers forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and the transforming power of the Holy Spirit.
He does not merely improve the appearance of a broken life.
He makes sinners new.
And the same Gospel that welcomed Gentiles into the people of God continues to call sinners from every background to repentance and faith.
There is no separate Savior for the religious person and the irreligious person.
No separate cross for the respectable and the disgraced.
No superior path of salvation for those raised in church.
No inferior Gospel for those who discovered Christ after years of rebellion.
There is one Lord Jesus Christ.
One saving grace.
One Gospel.
And one call to turn from sin and trust in Him.
If this truth is exposing something in your heart, do not rush past it.
Maybe you have been relying on your religious reputation.
Maybe you have been measuring other believers by customs God never made conditions of salvation.
Maybe you have been treating people from different backgrounds as though they must first become like you before they can truly belong to Christ.
Or maybe you have been trying to earn forgiveness that can only be received through faith in Jesus.
Whatever the struggle, bring it into the light.
You do not have to manufacture a testimony that sounds impressive.
You do not have to pretend your faith has never been shaken.
You can be honest before God.
There is room for sincere questions, honest struggles, and testimonies of God's faithfulness.
Because the Church was never meant to be a gathering of people pretending they saved themselves.
It is a community of people who need the mercy of Jesus Christ.
And that brings us to something else Acts 15 teaches us.
The Gospel is worth protecting.
Not through pride.
Not through hostility.
Not by treating every disagreement as though it makes someone an enemy.
But through faithful teaching, careful attention to Scripture, and a willingness to confront claims that compromise the sufficiency of Christ.
The early believers did not simply ignore the controversy and hope it would disappear.
They examined the matter.
They listened to testimony.
They considered Scripture.
They sought a faithful resolution.
And they communicated the decision to the churches.
Truth mattered because people mattered.
The spiritual welfare of Gentile believers mattered.
The unity of the Church mattered.
And the message of salvation through Jesus Christ mattered too much to be replaced by human additions.
That same responsibility belongs to Christians today.
We must learn to distinguish between biblical commands and human traditions.
Between the Gospel and cultural preferences.
Between genuine discipleship and religious gatekeeping.
Between salvation by grace and obedience as the fruit of faith.
And we must be willing to correct ourselves when Scripture reveals that we have confused those things.
Because sometimes spiritual maturity means discovering that a burden we placed on someone else was never ours to impose.
Sometimes repentance means admitting that we made our own religious preferences a test of another person's faith.
And sometimes the most Christ-honoring thing we can say is:
“I was wrong. God's Word does not require what I demanded.”
Imagine how many wounded believers might begin healing if we learned that kind of humility.
Imagine how many seekers might hear the Gospel more clearly if we stopped confusing Christianity with the traditions of our particular community.
Imagine how many people might finally understand that repentance is not an attempt to buy God's forgiveness, but a turning to the Savior who alone can forgive and restore.
This is why Gospel-centered teaching matters.
And it is why the mission of Gospel Warrior is more than publishing another Christian article.
We want people to open their Bibles.
To ask serious questions.
To understand Scripture in context.
To recognize false teaching.
To grow in holiness without losing sight of grace.
To know Jesus Christ more deeply than they know religious slogans.
And to become believers whose lives testify to the transforming power of the Gospel.
These resources are intended to help believers study, pray, reflect, and become more firmly rooted in biblical truth.
And if this article has helped you see Acts 15 more clearly, there is a meaningful way you can help that work continue.
Not because giving money purchases spiritual favor.
Not because a monthly payment replaces repentance, faith, or obedience.
But if you believe this ministry is helping people understand Scripture, encounter the Gospel, and grow as disciples, you can freely choose to support its continuation and expansion.
Those responsibilities deserve thoughtful consideration.
Scripture teaches us to give willingly, not under pressure.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
Not guilt.
Not fear.
Not a transaction for God's blessing.
But generosity flowing from love for Christ and concern for people who need to hear His truth.
These items are simply expressions of appreciation for those who choose to help sustain the ministry.
The deeper purpose remains unchanged.
Jesus Christ must be proclaimed.
Scripture must be taught faithfully.
And people must be pointed toward the Savior rather than toward any human personality, organization, or product.
Not merely to increase its reach.
But because somewhere among your friends and family may be someone quietly struggling with the very question Acts 15 answers.
Someone who believes Jesus died for sinners but cannot believe His grace is sufficient for them.
Someone who has been wounded by legalism.
Someone who has confused church traditions with the requirements of salvation.
Someone who has abandoned Christian fellowship because they were made to feel that their past could never be forgiven.
Or someone who has never understood why Jesus came at all.
You may not know who needs to read this.
But sharing it could begin a conversation about the Gospel that would never otherwise happen.
And invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, and even those who do not yet believe in Jesus to follow along.
Not so they can become followers of a ministry instead of Christ.
But so they can encounter more opportunities to hear and examine the truth about Him.
Because no Christian ministry should ever become the destination.
Jesus Christ is the destination.
And now, before you leave this story, return with me one final time to Jerusalem.
Picture the room.
Jewish believers who had known the covenant Scriptures from childhood.
Gentile believers whose lives had been transformed by the message of Israel's Messiah.
A controversy serious enough to threaten the peace of the Church.
A question that demanded an answer.
Must Gentiles become circumcised and keep the Law of Moses in order to be saved?
Peter stood and testified to what God had done.
Paul and Barnabas spoke of God's work among the nations.
James appealed to the prophetic Scriptures.
And the Church sent a letter affirming that Gentile believers were not required to bear that yoke as a condition of salvation.
But there was something even greater happening beneath that decision.
The early Church was learning to recognize the astonishing reach of God's grace.
The Messiah of Israel had opened the way for the nations to come to God.
The promises of Scripture were unfolding.
And people who had once been far off were being brought near through Jesus Christ.
Centuries later, we are still living in the light of that truth.
And the question Acts 15 raises is not merely what the Gentiles had to do.
It is what you are trusting to make you right with God.
Your religious background?
Your record of obedience?
Your reputation?
Your ability to avoid failure?
Your membership in a particular Christian community?
Or the crucified and risen Lord Jesus Christ?
Obedience matters.
Holiness matters.
Truth matters.
The Church matters.
But none of these can take the place of the Savior.
The Law reveals God's righteousness and exposes human sin.
The Gospel announces what God has accomplished through Jesus Christ for sinners who cannot save themselves.
And the Holy Spirit transforms those who belong to Him.
So stop trying to make your religious performance into a second savior.
Stop treating human traditions as though they possess the authority of God's Word.
Stop telling repentant sinners that the blood of Jesus is insufficient to cleanse them.
And if you have never truly placed your faith in Christ, hear His call today.
Turn from sin.
Believe the Gospel.
Trust the Savior who died for sinners and rose again.
Follow Him.
Not because you can make yourself worthy of His sacrifice.
But because He alone is worthy of your trust, your worship, and your life.
And if you already belong to Him but have been living under the crushing fear that His grace cannot reach your failures, remember what the apostles confessed:
“We believe that through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ we shall be saved...” (Acts 15:11, KJV)
Not through grace plus circumcision.
Not through grace plus human tradition.
Not through grace plus the illusion of personal perfection.
Through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ.
That is the Gospel worth defending.
That is the Savior worth following.
And that is the truth worth sharing with a world exhausted by the impossible task of saving itself.
Let it be a sincere confession of faith, not a performance for other people.
And carry this truth with you long after you close this article:
The cross was not where Jesus asked you to finish what you could never accomplish—it was where the Savior accomplished what you could never do for yourself.
